warmup.q: A tray holds five cookies, c1 to c5; c1, c3 and c5 are golden. This runs: tray.asSequence().filter { println("filter ${it.id}"); it.bake == GOLDEN }.map { println("map ${it.id}"); it.grams }.take(2).toList(). What prints?
options: filter c1 to filter c5, then map c1, map c3, map c5
filter c1, filter c2, filter c3, then map c1, map c3
Nothing: a sequence only runs when you print it
warmup.why: A sequence sends one cookie through the whole chain before it looks at the next. c1 passes the filter and goes straight on to map. c2 fails the filter. c3 passes and is mapped, and now take(2) has its two results, so nothing asks for c4 and c5. The first option is what the same chain prints on a List. toList() is what starts the work.

opening:
Picture an evening with a thick recipe book. You read the first recipe and ask one question: can I make this with what's in the fridge? No, so you turn the page. At the first yes, you close the book and start cooking. Nobody copies out all five hundred ingredient lists first, then checks every copy, then picks the first match.

Yet that's how the cookie trays in "Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends" worked. Each step finished the whole tray before the next step started. For two trays, nobody notices. For the recipe app's book of a million recipes, where each check is a slow call over the network, it means reading every page to find a recipe on page 518.

The trap is easy to miss, because the chain reads well and gives the right answer. Only the bill is wrong.

In this lesson, we'll count the work a list chain does, send one item at a time down the whole line with a sequence, make items on demand, and see where Java streams fit. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a recipe book and a cook who stops at the first recipe that fits. A list chain read every page anyway, because each step finished the whole tray first. A sequence sends one item down the whole line and stops when the answer is known, and a Java stream does the same, once.

Search your code for a list chain that ends in first, firstOrNull, any or take, and count what runs before it.

Next, we'll look at five tiny functions that run a block with one value in hand: let, run, with, apply and also. Which ones hand back the value, and which hand back the block's answer?

sections.h: A list chain finishes the whole tray before the next step starts
sections.html:
The recipe app keeps a big recipe book: a million recipes that its users have shared. Each evening it suggests one. To pick it, the app asks a matching service, a program on another computer that rates from 0 to 100 how well a recipe fits what's in your fridge. Each question takes about 2 ms, and the app pays for every one. Here's the search, written the way the last lesson taught us:

Java
Recipe firstMatch(List<Recipe> book, ToIntFunction<Recipe> matchScore) {
    List<Scored> scored = book.stream()
            .map(r -> new Scored(r, matchScore.applyAsInt(r)))   // about 2 ms per recipe
            .toList();
    List<Recipe> good = scored.stream().filter(s -> s.score() >= 90).map(Scored::recipe).toList();
    return good.isEmpty() ? null : good.get(0);
}
Kotlin
fun firstMatch(book: List<Recipe>, matchScore: (Recipe) -> Int): Recipe? =
    book.map { it to matchScore(it) }              // about 2 ms per recipe
        .filter { (_, score) -> score >= 90 }
        .map { (recipe, _) -> recipe }
        .firstOrNull()

it to matchScore(it) builds a pair: the recipe and its score, side by side. The chain reads well and gives the right answer. But say the first good match is recipe number 518. The chain still asks about all million recipes: 1,000,000 times 2 ms is 2,000 seconds, about 33 minutes of waiting for an answer that was ready after one second.

The cause is the tray from the last lesson. map and filter on a Kotlin List are eager: each one does its whole job at once. It loops over its whole input, writes every result into a brand-new list, and only then does the next step start. So the first map scores all million recipes and builds a list of a million pairs. filter builds a second list. Only then does firstOrNull look at element 0.

Java's collections have no eager chain, so the Java version above collects into a list after every step to do the same thing. Kotlin's List operations do exactly that for you.

The lambdas aren't the cost. As "Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out" showed, these functions are inline: the compiler pastes the loop and your lambda into the caller, so no lambda objects exist while the program runs. The cost is the lists. Every step allocates a new ArrayList, and a list of numbers holds each number as a separate boxed object. In a JMH run made for this course (JMH is a tool for timing small pieces of JVM code), a two-step filter { }.map { }.sum() over a million items allocated 26.5 MB per call.

For a short chain over a few hundred items, none of this matters, and the eager chain is the easiest to debug: you can stop after any step and look at a real list. It starts to matter when the input is big, a step is slow, or you only need the first few results.

A list chain runs every step on every item. Ask how many items you really need.

Let's watch the order of the work on one small tray first, then fix the search.

try.title: Watch the order of the lambdas
steps: Open OrderDemo.kt (or OrderDemoJava.java). The same filter, map and take(2) pick two golden cookies for a lunchbox, once from a List and once from a Sequence. Write down the print order you expect for each.
Run it with the command below.
In the List chain, move .take(2) up to right after tray. Predict how many filter lines print and what goes in the lunchbox, then run it.

code.title: OrderDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo enum class Bake { GOLDEN, RAW, BURNT } data class Cookie(val id: String, val grams: Int, val bake: Bake) /** One tray out of the oven: three golden cookies, one raw, one burnt. */ val tray = listOf( Cookie("c1", 45, Bake.GOLDEN), Cookie("c2", 90, Bake.RAW), Cookie("c3", 50, Bake.GOLDEN), Cookie("c4", 80, Bake.BURNT), Cookie("c5", 30, Bake.GOLDEN), ) /** Two golden cookies for a lunchbox, picked by a List chain and by a Sequence. Predict the print order first. */ fun main() { println("List chain:") val eager = tray .filter { println(" filter ${it.id}"); it.bake == Bake.GOLDEN } .map { println(" map ${it.id}"); it.grams } .take(2) println(" lunchbox $eager") println("Sequence chain:") val lazy = tray.asSequence() .filter { println(" filter ${it.id}"); it.bake == Bake.GOLDEN } .map { println(" map ${it.id}"); it.grams } .take(2) println(" built ${lazy::class.simpleName}, nothing has run yet") println(" lunchbox ${lazy.toList()}") }

alt.title: OrderDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo; import java.util.List; /** * The same three steps in Java. Java has no eager chain, so the "List chain" collects after every step, * which is exactly what Kotlin's List operations do. A Stream works like a Kotlin Sequence. */ public class OrderDemoJava { enum Bake { GOLDEN, RAW, BURNT } record Cookie(String id, int grams, Bake bake) {} static final List<Cookie> TRAY = List.of( new Cookie("c1", 45, Bake.GOLDEN), new Cookie("c2", 90, Bake.RAW), new Cookie("c3", 50, Bake.GOLDEN), new Cookie("c4", 80, Bake.BURNT), new Cookie("c5", 30, Bake.GOLDEN)); public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Collect after every step:"); List<Cookie> golden = TRAY.stream() .filter(c -> { System.out.println(" filter " + c.id()); return c.bake() == Bake.GOLDEN; }) .toList(); List<Integer> grams = golden.stream() .map(c -> { System.out.println(" map " + c.id()); return c.grams(); }) .toList(); System.out.println(" lunchbox " + grams.stream().limit(2).toList()); System.out.println("One Stream:"); var stream = TRAY.stream() .filter(c -> { System.out.println(" filter " + c.id()); return c.bake() == Bake.GOLDEN; }) .map(c -> { System.out.println(" map " + c.id()); return c.grams(); }) .limit(2); System.out.println(" built a stream, nothing has run yet"); System.out.println(" lunchbox " + stream.toList()); } }

try.expect: The List chain prints filter c1 to filter c5, then map c1, map c3, map c5: each step finishes the whole tray before the next starts. The Sequence chain first prints built TakeSequence, nothing has run yet, then filter c1, map c1, filter c2, filter c3, map c3. Cookies c4 and c5 are never looked at. Both lunchboxes hold [45, 50]. With take(2) first, the List chain filters only c1 and c2, and the lunchbox holds [45]. That's a different question (which of the first two cookies are golden), so moving a step changes the answer in both models. Laziness only changes how much work runs.

sections.h: A sequence sends one item at a time down the whole line
sections.html:
Put asSequence() in front of the same chain and the order of the work changes. A sequence is a lazy chain of steps. Lazy means it does no work until a result is wanted, and then only as much as that result needs.

Picture a kitchen line with two helpers: one checks each cookie's color, the next one weighs it. With a list, the checker goes through the whole tray before the weigher starts. With a sequence, the first cookie walks down the whole line, checked and then weighed, before the second cookie leaves the tray. When the lunchbox is full, the line stops, and the cookies still on the tray are never touched. The figure shows both orders for the lunchbox you just packed.

The work starts at a terminal operation, a step such as toList(), first(), sum() or count() that asks for items. Steps like map and filter are intermediate operations: on a sequence they only add a step to the plan. That's why the lunchbox program printed built TakeSequence, nothing has run yet before any cookie was checked. The sequence is in no hurry at all. It has written down the plan and will wait as long as you like for someone to ask.

Now the search. book.asSequence().map { ... }.filter { ... }.map { ... }.firstOrNull() asks the matching service 518 times and stops. This is short-circuiting: stopping as soon as the answer is known. first, firstOrNull, any, find and take(n) can do it, and in a lazy chain they stop every step above them too. For a single test you don't even need a sequence. book.firstOrNull { matchScore(it) >= 90 } is one inlined loop, and it also stops at 518.

How does it work underneath? Each intermediate operation on a sequence is an ordinary function, not inline, that wraps the sequence before it. map returns a TransformingSequence that holds your lambda, filter a FilteringSequence, take a TakeSequence. When the terminal operation asks the last wrapper for an item, that wrapper asks the one before it, and so on back to the list. Here is the heart of TransformingSequence in the Kotlin 2.4.21 standard library, next to the same idea written by hand in Java:

Java
Iterator<R> mapped = new Iterator<>() {
    public boolean hasNext() { return source.hasNext(); }
    public R next() { return transformer.apply(source.next()); }
};
Kotlin
override fun next(): R = transformer(iterator.next())
override fun hasNext(): Boolean = iterator.hasNext()

So a sequence trades the lists in between for one small wrapper object per step. The price is that the lambdas become real objects again, of the Function1 interface (created through invokedynamic, as "Function types, lambdas and closures" showed), and a number that passes through map is boxed on its way.

One kind of step breaks the line. sorted() and sortedBy { } can't hand out the smallest item until they've seen every item, so the first request makes them pull the whole input into a list and sort it. The kitchen picture breaks here too: no cook can say which cookie is the lightest by looking at one cookie. In the Try it, a sortedBy before firstOrNull { } pulls all 1,000,000 recipes, though the service still runs only 518 times. If you only need the smallest item, minByOrNull { } reads the input once and sorts nothing.

A sequence moves one item through every step and stops when the answer is known. Put the step that can stop at the end.

So far every item came from a list we already had. A sequence doesn't need one.

try.title: Count the work on a million recipes
steps: Read ScanCount.kt. Every line looks for the same recipe, number 518 of a million. For each line, predict how many times match runs and how many recipes the onEach counter pulls.
In the Sequence chain line, add .toList() just before .firstOrNull(). Predict the counts, then run it again.
Run the Java twin and compare findFirst on one stream with collecting first.

code.title: ScanCount.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo data class RecipeCard(val id: Long, val minutes: Int) /** A book of a million recipes. The first good match for tonight is number 518. */ private val book = List(1_000_000) { i -> RecipeCard(i + 1L, if (i % 1_000 == 517) 7 else 20 + i % 100) } private var scored = 0 private var pulled = 0 /** Stands for a call to the matching service: about 2 ms each in the app. Counts every call. */ private fun match(r: RecipeCard): Int { scored++; return if (r.minutes < 10) 95 else 10 } private fun report(label: String, found: RecipeCard?) { println("%-22s scored %,9d pulled %,9d found id %s".format(label, scored, pulled, found?.id)) scored = 0; pulled = 0 } fun main() { report("List chain", book.map { it to match(it) }.filter { it.second >= 90 }.map { it.first }.firstOrNull()) report("Sequence chain", book.asSequence().map { it to match(it) }.filter { it.second >= 90 }.map { it.first }.firstOrNull()) report("Sequence + sortedBy", book.asSequence().onEach { pulled++ }.sortedBy { it.id }.firstOrNull { match(it) >= 90 }) report("firstOrNull { }", book.firstOrNull { match(it) >= 90 }) }

alt.title: ScanCountJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.IntStream; /** The same search with Java collections and streams. The first good match is recipe number 518. */ public class ScanCountJava { record RecipeCard(long id, int minutes) {} record Scored(RecipeCard recipe, int score) {} static final List<RecipeCard> BOOK = IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000) .mapToObj(i -> new RecipeCard(i + 1L, i % 1_000 == 517 ? 7 : 20 + i % 100)) .toList(); static int scored = 0; static int pulled = 0; /** Stands for a call to the matching service. Counts every call. */ static int match(RecipeCard r) { scored++; return r.minutes() < 10 ? 95 : 10; } static void report(String label, RecipeCard found) { System.out.printf("%-22s scored %,9d pulled %,9d found id %s%n", label, scored, pulled, found == null ? null : found.id()); scored = 0; pulled = 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Scored> all = BOOK.stream().map(r -> new Scored(r, match(r))).toList(); // collect first, like a List chain report("Collect, then search", all.stream().filter(s -> s.score() >= 90).map(Scored::recipe).findFirst().orElse(null)); report("One Stream", BOOK.stream().map(r -> new Scored(r, match(r))).filter(s -> s.score() >= 90) .map(Scored::recipe).findFirst().orElse(null)); report("Stream + sorted", BOOK.stream().peek(r -> pulled++).sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(RecipeCard::id)) .filter(r -> match(r) >= 90).findFirst().orElse(null)); } }

try.expect: The List chain scores all 1,000,000. The Sequence chain and firstOrNull { } score 518 and stop. The sortedBy line also scores only 518, but its counter shows it pulled all 1,000,000 recipes into a list to sort them first. With .toList() added, the Sequence scores 1,000,000 again: toList() is a terminal operation that wants every item. Java prints the same numbers, because a stream is lazy in the same way and a collected list is not.

sections.h: Making items on demand: generateSequence and sequence { yield }
sections.html:
A sequence can make its items as it goes. Two builders produce an item only when someone asks for the next one.

generateSequence(seed) { next } starts from the seed and works out each item from the one before. It ends when the lambda returns null. The app's serving buttons, for 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 servings, are one line:

Java
List<Integer> servings = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 16, n -> n * 2).toList();   // [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]
Kotlin
val servings = generateSequence(1) { (it * 2).takeIf { next -> next <= 16 } }
servings.toList()   // [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]

takeIf returns the value when the test passes and null when it doesn't (lesson 6 covers it). Without the takeIf, the sequence never ends. That's fine as long as something downstream stops it, such as take(5) or first { }.

sequence { } is for items that take real code to make, like a recipe website that shows its search results one page at a time. Inside the block, yield(x) hands out one item and yieldAll(list) hands out many:

Java
Stream<SearchResult> results = Stream.iterate(1, page -> page <= 3, page -> page + 1)
        .flatMap(page -> fetchPage(page).stream());          // fetchPage is a web request
results.filter(r -> r.minutes() < 30).findFirst();           // also skips page 3 on JDK 21
Kotlin
val results = sequence {
    for (page in 1..3) yieldAll(fetchPage(page))   // fetchPage is a web request
}
results.first { it.minutes < 30 }                 // fetches page 1 and page 2, never page 3

You may wonder how a for loop can stop halfway and wait. The block is a suspend lambda: its type is suspend SequenceScope<T>.() -> Unit. A suspend function is one that can pause in the middle and carry on later, and the coroutines track covers them. The compiler turns the block into a small state machine, code that remembers which step it reached. Each yield saves where the block is and hands control back to whoever asked for an item. When they ask for the next one, the block carries on right after that yield. No second thread is involved: it all runs on the caller's thread, one step at a time. When nobody asks again, the block never carries on, so page 3 is never requested.

The block is restricted. Only yield and yieldAll may pause it. Call delay inside sequence { } and Kotlin 2.4.21 refuses: Restricted suspending functions can invoke member or extension suspending functions only on their restricted coroutine scope. For pages you must wait for without blocking a thread, use a Flow (the coroutines track).

The lab's version has one more rule: it doesn't know how many pages exist, and an empty page means the end. In Kotlin that's a while (true) loop with a break. In Java it's Stream.iterate(0, p -> p + 1).map(site::page).takeWhile(p -> !p.isEmpty()).flatMap(List::stream).

We now have three lazy pipelines: a list turned into a sequence, a generated one and a paging one. Java has a lazy pipeline of its own, and the two part ways at the edges.

try.title: Fetch only the pages you read
steps: Read Paging.kt. Each page holds three recipes, and later pages hold quicker ones. Predict which pages are fetched before the first recipe under 30 minutes prints.
Change first to firstOrNull and < 30 to < 1. Predict which pages are fetched and what prints, then run it.

code.title: Paging.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo data class SearchResult(val title: String, val minutes: Int) /** Stands for one web request to the recipe site: three results per page, quicker recipes on later pages. */ private fun fetchPage(page: Int): List<SearchResult> { println(" fetching page $page") return List(3) { i -> SearchResult("R$page-$i", 60 - (page * 3 + i) * 5) } } fun main() { // 1. a paging source: the block runs only as far as the consumer pulls val results = sequence { for (page in 1..3) yieldAll(fetchPage(page)) } println("first recipe under 30 minutes:") println(" ${results.first { it.minutes < 30 }}") // 2. the app's serving buttons: start at 1, double, and stop when the lambda returns null val servings = generateSequence(1) { (it * 2).takeIf { next -> next <= 16 } } println("servings: ${servings.toList()}") }

alt.title: PagingJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.IntStream; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** The same paging source and serving buttons with Java streams (JDK 9+ for the three-argument iterate). */ public class PagingJava { record SearchResult(String title, int minutes) {} /** Stands for one web request to the recipe site: three results per page. */ static List<SearchResult> fetchPage(int page) { System.out.println(" fetching page " + page); return IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> new SearchResult("R" + page + "-" + i, 60 - (page * 3 + i) * 5)).toList(); } public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. a paging source: a stream of page numbers, flattened into results Stream<SearchResult> results = Stream.iterate(1, page -> page <= 3, page -> page + 1) .flatMap(page -> fetchPage(page).stream()); System.out.println("first recipe under 30 minutes:"); System.out.println(" " + results.filter(r -> r.minutes() < 30).findFirst().orElseThrow()); // 2. the serving buttons: seed, condition to continue, next value List<Integer> servings = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 16, n -> n * 2).toList(); System.out.println("servings: " + servings); } }

try.expect: fetching page 1, fetching page 2, then SearchResult(title=R2-1, minutes=25). Page 3 is never fetched, because first stopped asking. Nobody has a recipe that takes under a minute, so with < 1 all three pages are fetched and it prints null: laziness can only save work when something stops early. The serving buttons are [1, 2, 4, 8, 16] in both languages.

aside.title: Can a sequence outlive the file it reads?
aside.html: Yes, and that's a trap. File("recipes.txt").bufferedReader().use { it.lineSequence() } looks as if it reads the file inside use { }. It doesn't. It returns a lazy plan for the reading, and use closes the file on its way out. The first terminal operation, somewhere else, reads from a closed file and fails with java.io.IOException: Stream closed. Either finish the work inside the block, with toList() if the lines fit in memory, or pass the work in, as File("recipes.txt").useLines { lines -> ... } does: it reads while the file is open and closes it afterwards. Java's Files.lines has the same shape, and whoever uses its stream must close it.

sections.h: Sequence or Stream, and when you need neither
sections.html:
A Java stream is Java's lazy pipeline: you make one from a collection with .stream(), add steps, and finish with a terminal operation. It runs in the same order as a sequence, one item at a time down the whole line, and the Java twins in this lesson print the same order and the same counts. The differences are practical.

A sequence is a recipe, not a tray of cookies. Each terminal operation follows the recipe again from the top, side effects included: call sum() and then count() on the same sequence and every map lambda runs twice. A few sequences refuse a second run. iterator().asSequence() and generateSequence { } without a seed throw IllegalStateException: This sequence can be consumed only once. A stream is always single-use, like a disposable piping bag: squeeze it once and it's spent. A second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed.

Streams can do things sequences can't. parallelStream() splits the work over several threads (paths of work that run at the same time), taken from a shared pool called the common ForkJoinPool. Sequences have no parallel mode at all. IntStream, LongStream and mapToLong keep numbers unboxed, and Kotlin has no LongSequence. On JDK 24 and later, gatherers add windows and running totals to streams (Go deeper has them).

Here are the numbers from the JMH run behind this course. The machine was a 4-core virtual machine shared with other work, so treat the times as rough, order-of-magnitude figures. The bytes allocated per call barely move between runs, so you can trust those. Each variant took a list of 1,000,000 items, kept the ones that passed a test (about 60% of them) and summed one Long from each:

Variant Time per call Allocated per call
for loop 5.2 ms about 0
filter { }.map { }.sum() on a List 148 ms 26,507,194 B
sumOf { if (passes) n else 0L } 2.6 ms about 0
asSequence().filter { }.map { }.sum() 9.0 ms 189 B
stream().filter().mapToLong().sum() 8.9 ms 428 B
stream().filter().map().reduce(0L, ...) 14 ms 28,782,178 B

The fastest line is neither a list chain nor a sequence. It's one fused sumOf, which is the hand-written loop. The sequence allocated almost nothing only because the JIT (the compiler inside the JVM that speeds up hot code while it runs) removed the boxes in this tiny benchmark. Don't count on that in a big program, where one call site sees many different lambdas. When the terminal operation could stop early (the first match was at index 101), the gap was huge: 141 ns for the sequence, 4.4 ms for the list chain.

So here's the rule I use. Use list operations by default. Switch to asSequence() when the end of the chain can stop early, or when a long chain runs over a big input. Use sequence { } or generateSequence for items made on demand, such as pages. Use a stream when you need parallel(), a primitive stream or a gatherer, or when a Java library hands you one.

Laziness saves work only when something stops early. When nothing does, one fused pass beats both.

That fused pass is sumOf, count { } or firstOrNull { }, and it's usually the shortest line too.

try.title: Read a sequence twice, and a stream twice
steps: Read Reuse.kt. Predict how many weigh lines print, and what the second read of once does.
In Reuse.kt, delete .asSequence() from weights. Predict how many weigh lines print now.

code.title: Reuse.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo data class Item(val name: String, val grams: Int) private val basket = listOf(Item("flour", 500), Item("sugar", 200), Item("butter", 250)) fun main() { // 1. a sequence is a recipe: every terminal operation runs the whole chain again val weights = basket.asSequence().map { println(" weigh ${it.name}"); it.grams } println("sum = ${weights.sum()}") println("count = ${weights.count()}") // 2. some sequences can be read only once val once = basket.iterator().asSequence() println("first read: ${once.map { it.name }.toList()}") try { once.toList() } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("second read: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: ReuseJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l05.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** A Java Stream is always single-use: the second terminal operation throws. */ public class ReuseJava { record Item(String name, int grams) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<Item> basket = List.of(new Item("flour", 500), new Item("sugar", 200), new Item("butter", 250)); Stream<Integer> weights = basket.stream().map(i -> { System.out.println(" weigh " + i.name()); return i.grams(); }); System.out.println("sum = " + weights.mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum()); try { System.out.println("count = " + weights.count()); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("count again: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } // to run it again, build a new stream from the source System.out.println("count = " + basket.stream().count()); } }

try.expect: Six weigh lines: three for sum() and three more for count(), because each terminal operation follows the recipe again. The sum is 950 and the count 3. The iterator-backed sequence fails on its second read with IllegalStateException: This sequence can be consumed only once. Java's stream fails on the second terminal operation with IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Without asSequence(), weights is a List built once, so weigh prints three lines in total.

compare.title: The first matches for a vegetarian guest: Sequence vs Stream

java.title: RecipeSearch.java
java.html: List<Long> firstMatchesFor(List<Recipe> book, ToIntFunction<Recipe> matchScore, int n) { return book.stream() .filter(Recipe::vegetarian) // the quick look first .filter(r -> matchScore.applyAsInt(r) >= 90) .map(Recipe::id) // boxed Long, as in Kotlin .limit(n) // stops early, like take(n) .toList(); // unmodifiable on JDK 16+ }

kotlin.title: RecipeSearch.kt
kotlin.html: fun firstMatchesFor(book: List<Recipe>, matchScore: (Recipe) -> Int, n: Int): List<Long> = book.asSequence() .filter { it.vegetarian } // the quick look first .filter { matchScore(it) >= 90 } .map { it.id } // boxed Long at the Function1 boundary .take(n) // stops early, like limit(n) .toList()

compare.note: Both pipelines are lazy and run in the same order, one recipe at a time, so both ask the matching service exactly as often. The real differences are at the edges. The stream can be used once; the sequence can be read again and will run the whole chain again. The stream could go parallel(); the sequence can't. Kotlin's terminal operations mirror the List API (firstOrNull returns null, and groupBy and sumOf are there), while the stream returns Optional from findFirst and needs Collectors for grouping. And on the Kotlin side you can drop asSequence() and get an eager List chain with the same code, which is often the better choice for small inputs.

worked.title: Decide whether a nutrition check should be lazy

steps.say: The app checks the 2 million ingredient lines in its recipe book against a nutrition table, and shows the first 20 lines whose ingredient the table doesn't know, so someone can add them. Here's the first version. Before reading on, find the step that makes laziness pay off.
steps.code: fun firstUnknown(lines: List<Line>, kcalPer100g: Map<String, Int>): List<Check> = lines.map { line -> Check(line.recipeId, line.ingredient, kcalPer100g[line.ingredient]) } .filter { it.kcal == null } .take(20)

alt.html: List<Check> firstUnknown(List<Line> lines, Map<String, Integer> kcalPer100g) { List<Check> all = lines.stream() .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), kcalPer100g.get(l.ingredient()))) .toList(); // 2 million objects return all.stream().filter(c -> c.kcal() == null).limit(20).toList(); }

steps.say: take(20) can stop early, so this chain should be lazy. 1. Ask the question: does the last step stop before the end? Here, yes. 2. Put asSequence() at the front. Now the chain builds 20 checks plus the known lines it read on the way, and no 2-million-item lists.
steps.code: fun firstUnknown(lines: List<Line>, kcalPer100g: Map<String, Int>): List<Check> = lines.asSequence() // 2. lazy from here on .map { line -> Check(line.recipeId, line.ingredient, kcalPer100g[line.ingredient]) } .filter { it.kcal == null } .take(20) // 1. stops early .toList()

alt.html: List<Check> firstUnknown(List<Line> lines, Map<String, Integer> kcalPer100g) { return lines.stream() // 2. one lazy pipeline .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), kcalPer100g.get(l.ingredient()))) .filter(c -> c.kcal() == null) .limit(20) // 1. stops early .toList(); }

steps.say: 1. Move the cheap test before the work. Building a Check for every line is wasted effort; test first and build the object only for real unknowns.
steps.code: lines.asSequence() .filter { it.ingredient !in kcalPer100g } // 3. cheap test, no object built .map { Check(it.recipeId, it.ingredient, null) } .take(20) .toList()

alt.html: lines.stream() .filter(l -> !kcalPer100g.containsKey(l.ingredient())) // 3. cheap test .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), null)) .limit(20) .toList();

steps.say: 1. Look for a barrier. Now someone asks for the 20 heaviest unknown lines, so the biggest gaps come first. That needs sortedByDescending { } before take(20), and the sort must read all 2 million lines first, so the sequence saves nothing over a List here. Keep whichever reads better, and know that the cost is the full pass plus the sort.
steps.code: lines.asSequence() .filter { it.ingredient !in kcalPer100g } .sortedByDescending { it.grams } // 4. reads everything .take(20) .map { Check(it.recipeId, it.ingredient, null) } .toList()

alt.html: lines.stream() .filter(l -> !kcalPer100g.containsKey(l.ingredient())) .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Line::grams).reversed()) // 4. reads everything .limit(20) .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), null)) .toList();

lab.title: Score only what you must, and fetch pages lazily
steps: Run the tests. Seven of nine fail. firstMatch already returns the right recipe, but the test shows it asks the matching service 200,000 times.
Fix firstMatch so it scores only up to the first match. Keep the signature.
Write firstMatchesFor: tonight's guest is vegetarian, so other recipes must never reach the service, and nothing may be scored after the nth match.
In ResultPages.kt, write allResults with sequence { }: ask for page 0, then 1, then 2, and stop at the first empty page.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read the last test and say what it shows about reading a sequence twice.
hints: For firstMatch, book.asSequence() in front of the existing chain is enough. So is book.firstOrNull { matchScore(it) >= 90 }, one inlined loop.
In firstMatchesFor, the order of the two filter calls decides which recipes reach the service. take(n) goes after both, before toList().
Inside sequence { } a while (true) loop is fine: break on an empty page, otherwise yieldAll(page). The loop pauses at every yieldAll until someone wants more.

drill.title: A paging source from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun <T> paged(fetch: (Int) -> List<T>): Sequence<T> that asks for page 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, and stops at the first empty page without asking for the next one. Then write the Java version that returns a Stream<T>. Check: does yours fetch anything before a terminal operation runs?

answer.html: fun <T> paged(fetch: (Int) -> List<T>): Sequence<T> = sequence { var page = 1 while (true) { val items = fetch(page++) // runs only when someone asks for more if (items.isEmpty()) break // an empty page ends it yieldAll(items) // pauses here between items } }

alt.html: static <T> Stream<T> paged(IntFunction<List<T>> fetch) { return Stream.iterate(1, page -> page + 1) // 1, 2, 3, ... lazily .map(fetch::apply) // one fetch per page, on demand .takeWhile(items -> !items.isEmpty()) // stops at the first empty page .flatMap(List::stream); }

recap: List operations are eager: each step loops over everything and builds a new list. They're inlined, so the cost is the lists and the boxed numbers, not lambda objects.
A sequence is lazy: nothing runs until a terminal operation asks, and then each item goes through every step before the next one is read.
Laziness pays when the end of the chain stops early (first, any, take). generateSequence and sequence { yield } make items on demand, on the caller's thread.
A sequence follows its recipe again on every terminal operation (a few are once-only); a Java stream is always single-use but can go parallel and stay unboxed.
Default to List operations. Use a sequence for early exits, long chains on big inputs and paging. One fused sumOf or firstOrNull { } beats both.
The limit: laziness can't help a step that needs everything. sorted reads the whole input first, and a chain with no early stop does all the work anyway.

explain.prompt: A teammate added .asSequence() in front of every collection chain in the recipe app "because sequences are faster". Explain in your own words what a sequence changes, and when it is worth it.
explain.answer: A sequence changes the order of the work. A List chain runs each step over the whole collection and builds a new list before the next step starts. A sequence runs nothing until a terminal operation asks for items, then moves each item through every step before reading the next. That saves the lists in between, and when the last step can stop early, like first or take, it skips the rest of the input entirely. It isn't free: each step becomes a wrapper object with a lambda, numbers get boxed on the way through, and a chain read twice does all its work twice. For a full pass over a few hundred items, the eager chain is just as fast and easier to debug, and a single sumOf or count { } beats both. I'd keep asSequence() where a chain stops early or runs several steps over large inputs, and take it out elsewhere.

deeper.html:
Three details matter once you write sequences in hot code, the code that runs most often.

Boxing. A sequence of Long is a sequence of java.lang.Long objects, because each step calls a Function1 whose invoke takes and returns Object. In bytecode, the lambda of map { it.grams.toLong() } is a Function1 whose invokedynamic signature returns Ljava/lang/Long;. Java's mapToLong takes a ToLongFunction that returns a primitive long. In the JMH run above, the sequence still allocated only 189 bytes per call, because the JIT's escape analysis saw that the boxes never left the method and removed them. That worked because the benchmark had one call site and one lambda type. In a big program the same FilteringSequence code runs with dozens of different lambdas, the call site becomes megamorphic (it sees too many types for the JIT to inline them), and the boxes come back.

IntelliJ's hint. The Kotlin plugin has an inspection that suggests turning a call chain on a collection into a sequence. It is on by default as a weak warning and fires for chains of five or more calls. Treat it as a prompt to ask this lesson's question (does the end of the chain stop early, and is the input big?), not as a rule.

Gatherers. Since JDK 24, streams have Stream.gather, with built-ins in java.util.stream.Gatherers: windowFixed, windowSliding, fold, scan and mapConcurrent. Kotlin has had the equivalents on both List and Sequence for years: chunked, windowed, fold and runningFold (also called scan). So a seven-day average of grams baked is days.windowed(7) { it.average() } in Kotlin, a hand-written loop in Java on JDK 21, and stream.gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(7)) on JDK 24 and later. The labs compile with release 21, so they use none of this.
